description: One separately authored practical instruction per exact original lesson for seven foundation courses. No original lessons changed.

units.title: CPU, memory, storage and processes — guided practice
units.scenario: Use task manager and operating-system architecture to classify CPU, memory, storage and process responsibilities.

sections.heading: Applied practice: CPU, memory, storage and processes
sections.command: Task Manager or system monitor → CPU, Memory, Disk, Processes
sections.instruction: Observe usage for one minute and explain why CPU time, memory occupancy and disk capacity measure different constraints.
sections.interpretation: A busy process is an observation, not evidence of malware.
sections.task: Identify two processes and which resource each consumes; describe the limitation of one screenshot.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Files, directories and permissions
sections.instruction: Create a directory map for a synthetic document and identify file owner, permissions and directory path.
sections.interpretation: A file path locates an object; owner and permissions control who may access it.
sections.task: Write the absolute path, a relative path and a least-privilege recommendation.

sections.task: Create a user/role matrix with one allowed and one denied action.

sections.heading: Applied practice: The terminal and command syntax

sections.interpretation: An exit code of zero means a command finished, not that a larger security goal is met.

sections.interpretation: A listed process may still be unresponsive or unable to accept requests.
sections.task: Specify a separate functional check that would establish a service is working.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Backups, updates and recovery
sections.instruction: After creating sample.txt in your own folder, preserve a backup and verify its bytes using hashes.
sections.interpretation: Identical hashes imply matching bytes, not an independently authenticated backup process.
sections.task: Write a restore checklist and identify what a successful restore must demonstrate.

units.title: Why professionals use terminals — guided practice
units.scenario: Explain command-line tools and permissions in a least-privilege investigation.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Why professionals use terminals
sections.instruction: Begin by executing whoami to identify the current account, pwd to identify the current folder, and ls to display only that folder. These commands are read-only observations useful before diagnosing or changing anything.
sections.interpretation: If the command outputs your own username and a path under /home, the session is likely running as your normal Linux user. A command prompt and account label do not establish permission to inspect another person's files.
sections.task: Produce a dated command log containing the exact three commands, their outputs, one reason each is useful, and one uncertainty you cannot resolve from this evidence alone.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: The present working directory — guided practice
units.scenario: Find and interpret the current working directory.

sections.heading: Applied practice: The present working directory
sections.instruction: Run pwd and record its value. Run cd ~ to move to your own Linux home and then pwd again; explain how the tilde expands to the current user's home and how a relative filename depends on the current working directory.
sections.interpretation: The first pwd may show /mnt/c on WSL when a Windows directory was inherited; the second should show the Linux home, such as /home/hp. The command does not move or alter files.
sections.task: Write the two resulting paths and give one absolute and one relative file reference pointing to a hypothetical notes.txt in your home directory. Explain why a mistaken directory can cause an overwrite.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Listing files and hidden entries — guided practice
units.scenario: List visible and hidden entries without editing data.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Listing files and hidden entries
sections.instruction: Enter your own disposable folder and compare ls with ls -la. Identify the file type and the owner/group/other permission columns, and explain why dotfiles appear only when hidden entries are included.
sections.interpretation: A leading dot only affects ordinary listing conventions; it is not encryption. The long listing also includes timestamps, ownership, mode and directory entries, none of which alone establishes malicious activity.
sections.task: Document two differences between the listings, interpret one mode string, and explain why you should inspect an unexpected hidden file without executing it.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Moving through directories — guided practice
units.scenario: Move deliberately through a safe folder tree.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Moving through directories
sections.instruction: Create a disposable nested folder with mkdir -p under your home. Use cd to enter it, pwd to confirm location, then cd .. to move exactly one directory upward; do not run commands in Windows system folders.
sections.interpretation: The path should end with /subfolder in the first pwd and /academy-paths after moving to its parent. The '..' path component navigates; it does not erase directories or change ownership.
sections.task: Provide the exact first and second paths, a diagram showing parent and child directories, and a description of what a relative reference to subfolder would resolve to.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Reading without modifying files — guided practice
units.scenario: Read content non-destructively and locate text evidence.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Reading without modifying files
sections.command: printf '%s\n' 'INFO boot complete' 'WARN retry' > ~/academy-paths/example.log; cat ~/academy-paths/example.log; grep -n WARN ~/academy-paths/example.log
sections.instruction: Only inside your own practice directory, use printf with redirection to create a synthetic two-line log. Read it with cat, then search WARN with grep -n; explain that writing the fixture is intentional and the later commands are read-only.
sections.interpretation: The grep result should include the warning's line number. A warning is a signal of an event, not a confirmed incident, and grep can miss relevant records when the search term is too narrow.
sections.task: Record the matched line number, copy the preceding and following synthetic events, and propose two competing explanations for the retry warning and a corroborating check for each.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Users, permissions and safe defaults — guided practice
units.scenario: Practice file permissions using a disposable artifact.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Users, permissions and safe defaults
sections.instruction: Use printf to create a disposable file under your home, apply chmod 600 only to that file, and verify the mode with ls -l. Break the value into owner 6 (read/write), group 0 and others 0.
sections.interpretation: The expected listing starts -rw-------. The owner still needs directory traversal permission to access the file, and Windows/WSL filesystem integration means this is not equivalent to full machine isolation.
sections.task: Create an access matrix for owner, group and others, record the actual mode output, and explain why chmod 777 or blanket sudo is not an acceptable repair for routine permission errors.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Processes and graceful troubleshooting — guided practice
units.scenario: Correlate processes with benign troubleshooting hypotheses.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Processes and graceful troubleshooting
sections.instruction: Execute ps -ef | head in your WSL training session and identify columns such as user, PID and command. Use it as a snapshot of visible processes rather than a substitute for endpoint or service health tests.
sections.interpretation: The list will vary with the system and may not include every process. A process being listed only establishes its existence at that moment; its backend dependencies or response handling may still fail.
sections.task: Record a selected harmless process name and PID, then design two non-destructive follow-up checks that could establish whether an associated service performs its intended function.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Command mistakes and recovery habits — guided practice
units.scenario: Recover from harmless errors without escalating privileges.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Command mistakes and recovery habits
sections.instruction: From the known training folder, deliberately list a nonexistent filename. Capture the error, then run pwd and ls to diagnose whether the problem is the current directory, filename or absent artifact.
sections.interpretation: The expected 'No such file or directory' response describes a failed path lookup, not a permission compromise. A nonzero command result calls for investigating the cause before retrying.
sections.task: Write a small error-response plan: verify cwd, inspect similar filenames, distinguish missing paths from access denied, then choose a safe corrective action without escalating privileges.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Windows accounts and profiles — guided practice
units.scenario: Inspect local accounts, groups and permissions without exporting personal data.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Windows accounts and profiles
sections.instruction: In Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt, run whoami /user and whoami /groups. Identify your own account SID and group memberships; redact personal identifiers from any training report shared with classmates.
sections.interpretation: The output shows identity and memberships at the time of the command. Effective access still depends on ACLs, deny rules and the requested resource, so membership alone is not proof of a successful access.
sections.task: Create a fictional user access profile listing a role, one allowed file operation, one prohibited privileged operation, and what evidence would confirm both outcomes.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Folders, paths and extensions — guided practice
units.scenario: Navigate Windows file paths and distinguish extensions from content types.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Folders, paths and extensions
sections.instruction: In PowerShell, first navigate to a disposable folder you own. Use Get-Location to confirm context and Get-ChildItem -Force to list hidden and normal entries without editing or launching unfamiliar files.
sections.interpretation: A .txt or .exe suffix influences Windows associations but is not a guarantee of file contents or safety. Force includes hidden entries and may reveal configuration files, not necessarily security findings.
sections.task: Document an absolute and relative Windows path, identify one hidden entry, and give two safe checks for an unknown file, such as inspecting properties and validating trusted provenance.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

sections.heading: Applied practice: Windows security updates
sections.command: Settings → Windows Update → View update history
sections.instruction: Review Windows Update history and record the relevant KB number, reported installation state and date. Plan how to confirm application functionality and restore data before any approved maintenance changes.
sections.interpretation: An update marked installed establishes an update event, not universal compatibility. A pending restart or failed update may affect the observed state and should be documented explicitly.
sections.task: Draft a change checklist with authorization, backup, rollback option, post-reboot build check and two application acceptance tests; perform no unapproved installation.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

units.title: Task Manager and services — guided practice

sections.heading: Applied practice: Task Manager and services
sections.command: Get-Process | Select-Object -First 10 Name,Id,CPU; Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10 Name,Status
sections.instruction: Use PowerShell's Get-Process and Get-Service to collect read-only snapshots. Record the process identifier, accumulated CPU time, service status and one question about whether a user-facing request actually works.
sections.interpretation: Get-Process CPU normally reports cumulative processor seconds, not current utilization percentage. A stopped service may be expected, and a running process can still have unhealthy dependencies.
sections.task: Record two process rows and two service rows, then propose a separate functional check and one log source that could distinguish a normal state from an outage.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.

sections.interpretation: Allow/deny entries interact with group membership and inherited permissions; one ACE in isolation does not demonstrate an actual successful access or a complete privilege evaluation.
sections.task: Draw a three-role access matrix for a fictional private file and state both a permitted read and an expected denied read that a qualified reviewer could validate.

sections.interpretation: Event identifiers can mean different things under different providers. A lone warning rarely establishes causality; review the provider's documented meaning and correlate other signals.
sections.task: Create a three-row fictional event timeline with source, timestamp, observation and uncertainty. Describe one alternate explanation and the next record that would help distinguish it.

sections.interpretation: A successful reboot only shows that the device started once. Recovery validation must include user data integrity, account access, security updates, device drivers and expected application transactions.
sections.task: Write a decision tree for a fictional failure with approval requirements, data backup prerequisites, post-repair functional checks and a stop condition to prevent accidental data loss.

sections.interpretation: Precision is 37.5%; recall is 60%, but sample quality and distribution matter.
sections.task: Recommend holdout validation and rollback criteria.
sections.safety: Practice only on synthetic files, owned computers or explicitly approved training environments. Observe first; avoid changing production configurations.
